page.title: National Wildfire Structure Loss Record
page.description: An NCEAS research project building a national record of buildings destroyed by wildfire, estimated from public satellite imagery and tested against official damage inspections.
page.og_description: Research estimates of building-by-building wildfire loss from public satellite imagery, tested against official damage inspections.

gate.tagline: Building a national record of the buildings that wildfires destroy, picking up where the U.S. Geological Survey’s record ends in 2022.
gate.access_text: This research program from the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS) at UC Santa Barbara and the Wildfire Resilience Index is shared privately.

lede: We are building a national record of the buildings that wildfires destroy, picking up where the U.S. Geological Survey's record ends in 2022. For each fire, a model compares public satellite images of the buildings that stood beforehand with images taken after, and calls each one destroyed or standing. These calls are research estimates, not inspections. Tested against official damage inspections, they are usually right for homes and other significant buildings in California wildfires, and weaker where we have had less inspection data to learn from, such as grass fires on the Great Plains. Damage records shared by fire agencies and partners are how we close those gaps.

popup.title: Why the model misses in Doyle
popup.lead: The 2021 Sugar fire burned through Doyle, a small town in California's high desert. In the area shown the model caught only 2 of 27 destroyed buildings; across the whole fire, 75 of 107.
reasons: Little vegetation: the buildings it missed had less greenery around them before the fire than the ones it caught, so their loss left a fainter mark in the satellite images. Grass fires on the Great Plains show the same problem.
Few examples to learn from: under 1 in 10 of the destroyed buildings in our records are in grassland or desert.
helps: More inspected damage records from open country, such as Oklahoma and the rest of the Great Plains, to train and test on.
More agencies and partners sharing their field damage records with us. Share yours.

items: Only buildings with a damage record are drawn. A building takes the record that falls inside its outline, or the nearest record within 10 m; if any record on it says destroyed, it counts as burned. Buildings whose only record is "Major (25–50%)" damage or "Inaccessible" are left off.

Damage records: CAL FIRE inspections for Palisades and Eaton; the U.S. Geological Survey record (Carlson et al. 2025) for Marshall and Sugar. A score of 0.88 or higher counts as "we said burned". On Sugar, buildings with no outline on record are drawn as small squares at the USGS point.

Palisades is scored by the model version used in our full Palisades check; Eaton, Marshall and Sugar by the leave-one-fire-out first call (September 2026). Tile counts cover the area inside the dashed line. Building outlines are pre-fire USA Structures outlines, except on Palisades, where they come from our Palisades check. The satellite base map is shown in grey so the building colors stand out.

sections.heading: Knowing what burned is slow, patchy and hard to compare
sections.lede: Fire agencies, recovery programs and researchers all need to know which buildings a wildfire destroyed. Field inspections are the most trusted answer, but they take crews and time, few are made public outside California, and the U.S. Geological Survey's national building-by-building record stops with the 2022 fires.

tiles.title: Inspections take crews and time
tiles.body: Field inspection is the gold standard, but it needs trained crews on the ground, and many fires never get one. CAL FIRE's public inspection data cover 443 fires from 2013 to 2025; outside California, the inspection records we could obtain cover only 55 fires.
tiles.src: CAL FIRE DINS open data (data.ca.gov), fires 2013-2025; non-California count as on the live page

tiles.title: Agencies record damage differently
tiles.body: Forms, building types and damage grades vary from agency to agency, so a loss count from one fire is hard to compare with another's.

tiles.title: The national record stops in 2022
tiles.body: The USGS building-by-building record covers 362 fires that destroyed 10 or more buildings from 2002 to 2022. Fires since then, including Eaton and Palisades in 2025, are not in it.
tiles.src: USGS data release doi:10.5066/P1QX6UXD (Carlson et al. 2025): destroyed buildings (bldg_cond B) counted per fire year

tiles.title: Free satellite images cover every recent fire
tiles.body: Europe's Sentinel-2 satellites have photographed the land since 2015, now about every five days, and the images are free. That lets us score every fire the same way, including where no crew went, though our estimates there are less tested.

steps.title: A call for each building
steps.body: The model compares Sentinel-2 satellite images of each building from before and up to 74 days after the fire and scores it 0 to 1; 0.88 or higher is a destroyed call. For some fires (62 so far), a refined second look follows about a year later.

steps.title: One consistent record
steps.body: A table and map of each listed building with its score and call, made the same way on every fire.

sections.heading: Accurate where it counts: homes and significant buildings
sections.lede: Scored against official building-by-building inspections (Lahaina: imagery-based labels), with each fire scored by a model version that never saw it. These scores measure the damage call alone; buildings missing from our list are covered under Limits.

stats.label: damage-call F1 on homes and other significant structures, all buildings pooled (0.91 averaged per fire)
stats.tip: Significant structures are houses, apartments, mobile homes, businesses, schools and churches: every inspected building except sheds and other utility structures, motor homes and infrastructure. On the 18 CAL FIRE incidents since 2023 with 10 or more destroyed buildings, the model caught 97% of those inspectors recorded as destroyed, and 97% of its destroyed calls were confirmed (F1 0.970). The refined second look scores 0.977 on 17 of the fires. Each fire was scored by a version of the model that never saw it. (The second look covers 17 of the 18 fires.)

items: Truth is CAL FIRE's building-by-building damage inspection, where destroyed means over 50% damaged; for Lahaina it is the BRIGHT 'destroyed' label, drawn from aerial imagery.
Each fire is scored by a model version trained without it; the CAL FIRE rows pool every scored building, so the largest fires weigh most.

These rows score the damage call alone. The significant-structure row scores it at each inspected building on the 8 largest fires and at the inspected buildings our list held on the 10 smaller ones; the Lahaina row scores it at each BRIGHT-labelled building. The single-family and other-building rows score it at the buildings our building list held at the time (87% of the destroyed single-family homes on those 15 fires; across 25 fires from 2024 on, the current list holds 93%, see above).

sections.footnote: All results are research estimates from a model, not official damage assessments. They cover homes and other significant buildings; sheds, garages and trailers are often missing from building maps (see Limits). See the full Palisades check →

sections.heading: Where we still need to improve
paragraphs: The model does best on what it was built for: homes and other significant structures in wildfires. By significant structures we mean the main buildings people live, work and gather in, such as houses, apartment buildings, businesses, schools and churches, as opposed to sheds, garages and other outbuildings.

It does worse in a few places. On grass fires on the Great Plains and in other open country, there is little vegetation around a building, so its loss leaves only a faint mark in the satellite images; the Sugar fire on the map shows the same problem in California's high desert. It is weaker outside California, because most of the inspection records we learn from are Californian. It misses more on fires that destroy only a few buildings. Mobile homes, trailers and sheds are often left out of the building maps we start from, so many go unscored. And it is not built for urban fires: one burned building among unburned ones is hard to see in 10 m satellite images.

These are the places we need to improve, and they all improve the same way: with more inspected damage records from the places and buildings where we do worst, and with time, as each new fire and each new year of imagery adds examples to learn from. If you hold damage records from fires like these, we would like to work with you.

sections.heading: Test it on your fires
sections.lede: The most useful help is field damage records from places we have not tested yet. In Jasper, Alberta (2024), 93% of the model's destroyed calls matched the town's own assessment.
sections.src: As published on the live page (version of 2026-11-09)

steps_card.title: A validation-only pilot
steps: You share field damage records for past fires, under your terms. We use them only for testing unless you agree otherwise.
We run the unchanged model on those fires.
You get a building-by-building comparison with your records. We publish only aggregate results.

contact_card.title: A record for your region
contact_card.body: If a pilot works well, the same method could build a long-term loss record for a state, province or country. We welcome introductions to agencies, researchers and funders.

sections.disclaimer: Scientific research by the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS) at UC Santa Barbara, shared for information only. Results are estimates from a research model, not official damage assessments or inspections; do not use them in an emergency or as the sole basis for a decision about a property.
